title: Predicting Population Genetic Patterns
subtitle: Personalised genetic risk: what it can predict, and what it can't
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the use of data analysis from a large-scale collaborative project to identify trends, patterns and relationships, for example: population genetics studies used to determine the inheritance of a disease or disorder (ACSBL064, ACSBL073)
Discuss the risks and benefits of using biotechnologies to provide personalised information about the risk of developing, and management of, a non-infectious disease
Assess potential limitations and constraints of SNP testing and databases in diagnostic medicine
inquiryQuestion: Can population genetic patterns be predicted with any accuracy?
lessonIntent: Students can explain why population genetic data predicts group trends better than individual outcomes, describe how single gene tests and polygenic risk scores give personalised risk information for non-infectious diseases, and discuss the benefits and risks of that information.
examSkill: Discuss a personalised genetic test by giving benefits for risk and management, risks for the individual and family, and a conclusion that keeps probability separate from certainty.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome to HSC Science. This is HSC Biology. Today, personalised genetic risk, and what population genetics can really predict. Let's get into it.

scenes.heading: Your risk, in the mail
scenes.body: Spit in a tube, post it off, and an app reports your genetic risk for diseases like breast cancer and heart disease.
scenes.callout: What can a genetic risk result really tell you, and who else does it affect?
scenes.caption: Personalised genetic risk tests are widely available, and every result also says something about relatives.

voiceover.text: OK, here's something anyone can do today. Order a genetic test online, spit into a tube, post it off, and a few weeks later an app tells you your genetic risk for conditions like breast cancer, heart disease or Alzheimer's disease. Millions of people have done exactly that. But that result isn't only about you. You share about half your DNA with each parent, each brother or sister, and each child, so your result says something about them too, and they never agreed to be tested. So what can personalised genetic information really tell you about a disease that isn't infectious, like cancer or heart disease? What are the benefits, and what are the risks? That's today's question, and it rests on the most important rule in population genetics. Genetic risk is not genetic destiny.

scenes.heading: Trends predict better than individuals
scenes.body: Population genetic data predicts patterns across groups far more reliably than the outcome for any one person.

bullets.text: Reliable: risk patterns in groups and families, and allele frequency trends.
Uncertain: whether one particular person will develop a disease.
Environment, other genes and chance all shape an individual's outcome.

scenes.secondary: A risk variant raises the probability of a disease. It doesn't guarantee it. Match the scope of your claim to the scope of your data.
scenes.callout: Higher probability is not a certain outcome.
scenes.caption: Population data predicts group trends reliably; individual outcomes stay probabilistic.

voiceover.text: Let's start with what population genetics is actually good at. Its real strength is predicting trends across groups. Things like how much more common a disease is in families that carry a certain variant, or how allele frequencies differ between populations. Those predictions rest on data from thousands of people, so they're reliable. What it's much less good at is predicting what will happen to one particular person. That's because an individual's outcome also depends on their environment, their lifestyle, their other genes and plain chance, and none of those are fixed by one variant. So a risk variant raises the probability of a disease, but it doesn't guarantee it. The rule that follows is simple. Population level evidence supports population level conclusions, so match the scope of your claim to the scope of your data.

scenes.heading: Two kinds of personalised risk test
scenes.body: Biotechnology gives personalised risk information in two main ways, with very different strengths.

bullets.text: Single gene tests: sequence genes like BRCA1, BRCA2 or LDLR for high impact variants.
Polygenic risk scores: combine hundreds of SNPs, each with a tiny effect, into one estimate.
Both are used to guide management: screening, medication, lifestyle or surgery.

scenes.callout: Big effect from one gene, or small effects from many SNPs.
scenes.caption: Single gene tests find high impact variants; polygenic scores add up many small SNP effects.

voiceover.text: So how does biotechnology actually give someone personalised risk information? There are two main kinds of test. The first is a single gene test, where genes like BRCA1 and BRCA2 for breast and ovarian cancer, or LDLR for inherited high cholesterol, are sequenced to look for variants with a big effect. Carrying one of those can change your risk enormously. The second is a polygenic risk score. That combines hundreds or even thousands of SNPs, each with a tiny effect on its own, into a single estimate of risk for a common disease like heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Those scores usually shift risk only a little. And either way, the point is management. The result can guide earlier or more frequent screening, medication, lifestyle changes, and in some cases preventive surgery.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Non infectious disease: a disease not caused by a pathogen, like cancer or heart disease.
Personalised risk information: an estimate of one person's disease risk from their own DNA.
Polygenic risk score: a combined risk estimate from many SNPs of small effect.
Genetic counselling: expert support to understand a genetic test and its implications.
Uncertainty: the limit on how exact a prediction can be, even with strong evidence.

scenes.callout: A risk estimate is a probability, never a diagnosis.
scenes.caption: Non infectious disease, personalised risk information, polygenic risk score, genetic counselling, uncertainty.

voiceover.text: Let's pin down the words. A non infectious disease is one that isn't caused by a pathogen, like cancer, heart disease or type 2 diabetes. Personalised risk information is an estimate of one person's risk of a disease, based on their own DNA. A polygenic risk score is a combined estimate built from many SNPs, each with a small effect. Genetic counselling is expert support that helps someone understand a genetic test before and after they take it, including what it means for their family. And uncertainty is the limit on how exact any prediction can be, even when the evidence is strong. That last word is the heart of this lesson. Strong evidence reduces uncertainty, but it never removes it.

scenes.heading: Benefits and risks of knowing
scenes.body: Personalised genetic information can save lives, but it can also mislead, worry or expose people.

bullets.text: Benefit: early prevention, like cholesterol lowering drugs for familial hypercholesterolaemia, and early testing of relatives.
Risk: false reassurance from limited tests, or anxiety from uncertain results.
Risk: privacy, family disclosure and possible discrimination, for example by insurers.

scenes.callout: The value of a result depends on what you can do with it.
scenes.caption: Benefits: prevention, family testing, matched treatment. Risks: misleading results, anxiety, privacy.

voiceover.text: Now the discussion the syllabus asks for, benefits and risks. The biggest benefit is targeted prevention. Take familial hypercholesterolaemia, which affects about one in two hundred and fifty people and causes very high cholesterol from birth. A genetic diagnosis means treatment with cholesterol lowering drugs can start early, long before a heart attack. A second benefit is that relatives can be tested and managed early too. But there are real risks. A consumer test that checks only a few variants can give false reassurance, while a variant of uncertain meaning can cause anxiety for nothing. Results can also reveal things about family members who never consented, and there are concerns about privacy and genetic discrimination, for example by insurers. So the value of a result depends on what you can actually do with it, and that's why genetic counselling matters.

scenes.heading: Discuss a BRCA test
scenes.question: A 30 year old woman's mother developed breast cancer at 40. She is considering a BRCA1 and BRCA2 test. Discuss the benefits and risks of this personalised information.
scenes.coachNote: Discuss means both sides. Cover risk and management for her, effects on family, and the limits of the result.
steps: Benefit: a harmful BRCA variant raises lifetime breast cancer risk to roughly 70%, so she could start earlier MRI screening or consider preventive options.
Benefit: her relatives could then be tested for the same family variant.
Risk: a positive result can cause anxiety, and reveals information about relatives who didn't consent.
Risk: a negative result doesn't mean zero risk, and some results are variants of uncertain significance.
Conclusion: valuable when paired with genetic counselling, as long as it's read as risk, not certainty.
scenes.caption: A BRCA test can guide screening and family testing, but results are risks, not certainties.

voiceover.text: Let's work through a discuss question. A thirty year old woman's mother developed breast cancer at forty, and she's considering a BRCA one and BRCA two test. Discuss the benefits and risks. Discuss means both sides, so let's build it. The first benefit is management. If she carries a harmful BRCA one variant, her lifetime risk of breast cancer is roughly seventy percent, so she could start MRI screening earlier and consider preventive options. The second benefit is for her family, because relatives could then be tested for that exact variant. Now the risks. A positive result can cause real anxiety, and it reveals information about relatives who never agreed to it. And a negative result doesn't mean zero risk, since she still has the ordinary risk every woman has, and some results come back as variants of uncertain significance. So the conclusion is that the test is valuable when it comes with genetic counselling, as long as it's read as a risk, not a certainty.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: 'I carry the variant, so I will get the disease.' Most variants raise risk. Even BRCA1 gives roughly a 70% lifetime breast cancer risk, not 100%.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: 'My test was clear, so I'm safe.' A test only reads the variants it checks, and most cancers and heart disease happen in people with no high risk variant at all.
scenes.callout: Positive isn't destiny; negative isn't immunity.
scenes.caption: A risk variant raises probability, not certainty; a clear test only covers the variants it read.

voiceover.text: Two traps that cost marks. Trap one, thinking that carrying a disease variant means you'll definitely get the disease. For almost every variant that's wrong. Even BRCA one, one of the strongest risk variants known, gives roughly a seventy percent lifetime risk of breast cancer, which is high, but it isn't one hundred percent. Environment, other genes and chance still matter. Trap two is the mirror image. Thinking that a clear test means you're safe. A test only reads the variants it checks, and most cases of cancer and heart disease actually happen in people who carry no high risk variant at all. So a positive result isn't destiny, and a negative result isn't immunity. Keep your wording precise about the trend, and cautious about the person.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A company's report says: 'Your polygenic risk score is in the top 10%. You will develop heart disease.' Rewrite this so it is accurate, and suggest one sensible use of the result.
answerSteps: The original turns a probability into a certainty, which is an overclaim.
Use probability language: a higher than average estimated risk, compared with the reference population.
Note that lifestyle, other genes and chance also affect the outcome, and scores are less accurate for some ancestries.
Use: earlier cholesterol and blood pressure checks and lifestyle changes, discussed with a doctor.
Answer: 'Your estimated risk is higher than average, but this doesn't mean you will develop heart disease.' ✓
scenes.caption: Rewrite as a higher estimated risk, not a certainty, and use it to guide earlier checks.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A company's report says, your polygenic risk score is in the top ten percent, you will develop heart disease. Rewrite that so it's accurate, and suggest one sensible use of the result. Pause and rewrite it yourself. OK. First, spot the error. The report turns a probability into a certainty, which is a clear overclaim. To fix it, use probability language, like your estimated risk is higher than average, compared with the population the score was built from. Then add that lifestyle, other genes and chance also affect the outcome, and that these scores are less accurate for people whose ancestry wasn't well represented in the original data. As for a sensible use, it could prompt earlier cholesterol and blood pressure checks and some lifestyle changes, talked through with a doctor. So a good version reads, your estimated risk is higher than average, but this doesn't mean you will develop heart disease.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Population data predicts group trends reliably, individual outcomes only as probabilities.
Single gene tests find high impact variants; polygenic scores add up many small SNP effects.
Benefits: targeted screening and prevention, and testing of relatives.
Risks: false reassurance, anxiety, uncertain results, privacy and discrimination.
Genetic risk is not genetic destiny: positive isn't certain, negative isn't zero.
scenes.finalPrompt: Discussing a genetic test? Give a benefit for managing risk, a risk for the person or family, then keep probability separate from certainty.
scenes.caption: Five takeaways: trends versus individuals, two kinds of test, benefits, risks, risk isn't destiny.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. Five things to take away. First, population genetic data predicts group trends reliably, but individual outcomes only ever as probabilities. Second, single gene tests look for high impact variants like those in BRCA1, while polygenic risk scores add up the small effects of many SNPs. Third, the benefits are targeted screening and prevention, and the chance to test relatives early. Fourth, the risks include false reassurance, anxiety, results of uncertain meaning, and concerns about privacy and discrimination. And fifth, genetic risk is not genetic destiny, so a positive result isn't certain and a negative one isn't zero. When you discuss any genetic test, give a benefit for managing risk, a risk for the person or their family, and keep probability separate from certainty.
